problem_plain: Modern AI models are enormous: a single large language model may store tens of billions of numbers, each occupying 16 or 32 bits of memory. Every time the chip runs a calculation it must move those numbers from storage into the compute units, and that movement is far slower and more energy-hungry than the arithmetic itself. Quantization is the practice of re-encoding each number using fewer bits — say 4 instead of 16 — so the same wire can carry more values per second and the same memory chip can hold a larger model.
why_plain: Memory bandwidth is a physical bottleneck: the wires connecting storage to arithmetic circuits can only move a fixed number of bits per second, and that limit has grown far more slowly than model size. Shrinking each number means more of the model fits in fast on-chip memory and fewer trips are needed to slow off-chip storage.
approach_plain: Researchers replace high-precision numbers (32-bit or 16-bit floating point) with compact codes — integers, lookup-table indices, or custom small formats — then either retrain the model to absorb the rounding error, or design the chip arithmetic to match the new format directly. The hard part is that not all numbers in a model are equally important: a few extreme 'outlier' values carry disproportionate information and break naive compression. Most papers therefore pair a compression algorithm (which finds or avoids the outliers) with a matched hardware unit (which knows how to work in the compressed format without first converting back to the original).

groups.heading: Making the number format itself smarter
groups.explain: Instead of forcing every weight or activation into a fixed 4-bit or 8-bit integer, these papers design new numerical formats that adapt to the actual spread of values in a given layer or group of weights. A standard integer grid wastes most of its codes on values that never appear; an adaptive format places its grid lines where values actually cluster, squeezing more accuracy from the same number of bits.

papers.name: M-ANT
papers.gloss: Adapts the numeric encoding independently for each small group of 128 weights so each group gets the grid that fits its own distribution; handles the model's running memory (the record of past tokens) in real time using the same adaptive hardware; up to 4.46x faster than a prior state-of-the-art accelerator.

papers.name: Anda
papers.gloss: Defines a new number type where each group of activations shares one exponent but each element gets a dynamically allocated mantissa length, tuned per model layer without retraining; 2.4x faster and 3.1x more energy-efficient than a standard floating-point baseline.

papers.name: MX+
papers.gloss: Fixes a flaw in the industry-standard MX (Microscaling) 4-bit format: the single extreme value in each 32-element block was encoded with only 1 mantissa bit, causing large errors; MX+ steals unused bits in that element's own encoding to give it 3 mantissa bits, recovering up to 42 percentage points of accuracy with near-zero storage overhead.

papers.name: FATE
papers.gloss: Applies different numeric precisions to different dimensions of a hyperdimensional computing classifier (a pattern-matching technique that uses very long binary vectors), using the observation that some dimensions matter more than others; targets low-power embedded FPGAs, though headline numbers are not yet available.

groups.heading: Compressing the model's running memory (KV cache)
groups.explain: When a language model reads a long document or conversation, it builds up a 'running notes' buffer — called the KV cache — that records the context of every token it has seen. This buffer grows with context length and is read on every generation step, consuming a large fraction of memory bandwidth. Compressing these stored notes from 16 bits to 4 bits cuts the bandwidth cost of long contexts roughly 4x, but the notes contain the same outlier problem as weights.

papers.name: Oaken
papers.gloss: Profiles each model layer's note distributions in advance (once, offline) to learn outlier thresholds, then applies those thresholds at runtime to split each note vector into three groups and quantize each group to 4 or 5 bits; stores outliers in a sparse format that piggybacks on the dense 4-bit block, cutting outlier storage from 23 to 8 bits per entry; 1.79x throughput over a standard server at batch size 256.

papers.name: COMET
papers.gloss: Quantizes both model weights and the running notes to 4 bits simultaneously (W4A4KV4), keeping occasional large activation values at 8 bits in a mixed-precision layout; a custom GPU compute kernel handles both precisions in one pass; 2.88x faster kernel throughput and 2.02x end-to-end throughput over a standard serving library on A100.

papers.name: QServe
papers.gloss: Uses a two-stage weight quantization (first 8-bit, then 4-bit) with a protected numerical range that guarantees no overflow when the GPU's tensor cores operate in 8-bit mode; absorbs the scale needed for 4-bit note compression into the preceding weight matrix so no extra work is needed at runtime; up to 3.5x more throughput than a vendor-optimized baseline on NVIDIA L40S.

groups.heading: Lookup tables instead of multiply units
groups.explain: When weights are compressed to 2 or 3 bits, there are so few possible values that instead of multiplying an input by a weight, you can simply look up the answer in a small table. A table lookup is far cheaper in silicon area and energy than a floating-point multiplier. These papers build both the training recipes and the specialized hardware needed to make lookup tables a viable replacement for conventional arithmetic.

papers.name: LUT Tensor Core
papers.gloss: Redesigns the GPU's matrix-multiply engine as a bit-serial lookup table: weights are re-encoded so half the table entries cancel by symmetry, and software fuses the table-building step with an adjacent layer's computation to hide its cost; 2 to 5.5x end-to-end inference speedup; 4 to 6x smaller area than a conventional floating-point multiply unit at the same silicon node.

papers.name: FIGLUT
papers.gloss: Pre-computes all possible products of a floating-point input value with every possible low-bit weight pattern and stores them in a half-size lookup table; at inference time the hardware indexes the table by the weight bits rather than multiplying; 59% higher energy-efficiency than a prior lookup-table chip at the same 3-bit precision.

papers.name: LUT-DLA
papers.gloss: Replaces multiply-accumulate units entirely with lookup-table fetch-and-accumulate units trained using a multi-stage algorithm; achieves sub-1-bit-equivalent compression (representing groups of values with shared codebook entries); 1.4 to 7x better power efficiency and up to 146x better area efficiency than scalar quantization hardware.

papers.name: VQ-LLM
papers.gloss: Solves the slow GPU memory access pattern that made lookup-table (vector quantization) LLM inference slower than plain 16-bit inference: caches hot codebook entries in thread-private registers (eliminating conflicts), partitions computation along codebook boundaries, and fuses data shuffling with an intra-warp instruction; reduces latency 64 to 99% versus prior vector-quantization implementations.

groups.heading: Grouping weights together before compressing (vector quantization)
groups.explain: Instead of rounding each weight independently, vector quantization takes a small group of weights (say 8 or 16 at a time) and replaces the whole group with a single code that points to the nearest matching group in a learned dictionary. This allows the dictionary to capture the joint structure of the weights, achieving higher compression at the same accuracy. The challenge is that building the dictionary (a k-means clustering step) is expensive, and the wrong dictionary entries hurt accuracy badly.

papers.name: MVQ
papers.gloss: Combines structured pruning (removing every other weight in a regular pattern) with a dictionary-building algorithm that ignores the pruned zeros so they cannot distort the dictionary entries; the paired accelerator skips the pruned positions in its compute array, cutting the systolic array's area by 55% and improving energy efficiency by 2.3x over the baseline.

papers.name: eDKM
papers.gloss: Makes train-time weight clustering tractable for 7-billion-parameter language models by deduplicating and sharding the large temporary tensors that must be kept in CPU memory during the backward pass; reduces per-layer memory 130x, shrinking a 7B model from 12.6 GB to 2.5 GB at 3 bits per weight.

papers.name: BitMoD
papers.gloss: Assigns each group of 128 weights its own numeric type, chosen from a small family of formats, and processes all types through a single bit-serial hardware datapath; avoids separate hardware for each format; reportedly 1.69x faster than a prior adaptive-quantization accelerator at under 0.5% accuracy loss.

groups.heading: Fitting quantization into existing chip architectures
groups.explain: Most deployed hardware — GPUs, CPUs, FPGAs — was not designed for 3-bit or 4-bit arithmetic. These papers bridge the gap by designing software kernels, instruction-set extensions, or small hardware additions that let existing chips run quantized models efficiently without a complete redesign.

papers.name: DECA
papers.gloss: Adds a small hardware block beside each CPU core that decompresses quantized and sparsified weight tiles in a three-stage pipeline (decode → de-sparsify → scale), hiding the decompression work behind a new speculative load instruction; on a server CPU running a 70-billion-parameter model the decompression was consuming 95% of instructions — DECA eliminates that bottleneck, giving 1.6 to 2.6x faster token generation.

papers.name: CAMP
papers.gloss: Adds a small hierarchical multiplier extension to ARM and RISC-V vector units so they can run 4-bit and 8-bit integer matrix math natively; uses only 1-4% extra chip area; achieves up to 23x speedup over an unmodified vector core on quantized matrix multiply.

papers.name: HiPACK
papers.gloss: Solves the mismatch between 4-bit weights and 8-bit ARM SIMD registers by pre-expanding packed sub-8-bit data before the multiply loop, then using an interleaved register arrangement so a single SIMD instruction can process two packed streams simultaneously; up to 4.6x faster than a floating-point baseline on a Raspberry Pi 4 processor.

papers.name: MEADOW
papers.gloss: Enables 8-bit quantized language model inference on a 10-watt FPGA by sequencing attention computation across heads rather than materializing all at once, and by packing weights with frequency-aware reindexing to minimize off-chip memory trips; 1.5x faster decode and 2.5x faster prefill over a naive implementation.

papers.name: MiLo
papers.gloss: Compresses mixture-of-experts language models (which activate different sub-networks per token) to 3-bit weights using calibration-free quantization, then adds small low-rank correction matrices that repair accuracy; the 3-bit GPU kernel uses zero-wasted bit packing and supports batch sizes above 1, which prior 3-bit kernels could not; 1.2x throughput over the previous best backend.

papers.name: HyC-LoRA
papers.gloss: Compresses the activation buffers needed during fine-tuning (adapting a pre-trained model to a new task) to near 2 bits on average, using structured outlier preservation for non-linear operations and reordering compute so some buffers can be recomputed rather than stored; targets on-device fine-tuning on a single GPU.

groups.heading: Quantization for specialized or non-language workloads
groups.explain: The quantization challenge extends beyond language models to protein structure prediction, image-generation diffusion models, ray tracing in graphics, vector similarity search, and even the voltage stability of the chip itself. Each workload has its own data distribution and memory access pattern, requiring its own quantization strategy.

papers.name: LightNobel
papers.gloss: Handles the quadratically growing activation tensor in protein structure prediction (AlphaFold, ESMFold) by classifying activations into three groups based on magnitude and applying INT4 to ordinary values and INT16 only to outliers; a reconfigurable hardware matrix unit dynamically assigns compute lanes to each precision mix; 8.44x faster than an A100 GPU on the most expensive computation, with peak memory cut by 120x for long protein sequences.

papers.name: Ditto
papers.gloss: Exploits the fact that adjacent denoising steps in an image-generation diffusion model produce very similar outputs: the difference between steps is small and can be encoded in very few bits, often zero; a co-designed accelerator skips zero-difference computations; reportedly up to 1.5x faster with 17.7% energy savings, though details are limited.

papers.name: AQB8
papers.gloss: Compresses the spatial bounding-box hierarchy used in ray tracing (the tree of boxes that determines which triangles a light ray might hit) to 8-bit integers at multiple hierarchy levels, so intersection tests run in integer arithmetic end-to-end with no conversion back to floating point; 1.82x faster than a GPU ray-tracing unit with 49% less energy and 70% fewer off-chip memory accesses.

papers.name: Panacea
papers.gloss: Addresses a subtle incompatibility between asymmetric quantization (which gives better accuracy) and bit-slice computation (which skips zero slices for efficiency): asymmetric encoding produces many non-zero slices that a naive skip engine would miss; Panacea deliberately shifts the zero point and selects bit slices to maximize skippable zeros; 1.97x more energy-efficient than a prior bit-slice accelerator.

papers.name: NeuVSA
papers.gloss: Unifies the neural embedding step and the approximate nearest-neighbor search step in vector database queries into a single hardware design by reformulating both as the same product quantization (grouping of vector components into codebook entries) operation; eliminates the data-format mismatch between the two stages; reportedly 2.82 to 416x lower latency than CPU and GPU baselines.

papers.name: AIM
papers.gloss: Addresses an unexpected consequence of running quantized workloads on dense SRAM compute-in-memory chips: the bit patterns of quantized weights determine how much electrical current spikes (IR-drop) occur inside the chip, which can cause errors; AIM adds a regularization term during quantization training that steers weights toward bit patterns with fewer '1' bits, reducing voltage spikes by up to 69% and improving chip throughput by 1.15x.

connect: Every paper in this theme is ultimately solving the same physical constraint: the wires that carry numbers between storage and arithmetic are the bottleneck, not the arithmetic itself. Quantization is the discipline of packing more information into each wire transfer — whether by shrinking individual numbers, replacing arithmetic with table lookups, or skipping redundant values entirely — so that chips can run larger models faster without waiting for data to arrive.
